fields.title: Statement by OCHA Sudan on recent attacks in West Kordofan State
fields.body:
***(Khartoum, 11 October 2026)*** OCHA is deeply concerned by reports of a deadly drone strike on 9 October that hit a building sheltering displaced families in An Nuhud, West Kordofan State. At least 12 civilians, including women and children, were reportedly killed and eight others injured.

On the same day, a drone strike in Ghubaish town reportedly killed five civilians, including three children, in a residential neighbourhood hosting displaced families.

These were people who had already been forced from their homes by conflict, only to face further violence in places where they had sought safety.

The increasing frequency of drone strikes across Sudan is deeply alarming, exposing civilians, including displaced families, to further death, injury and suffering.

International humanitarian law must be respected, and civilians and civilian infrastructure protected. People fleeing violence must be able to find safety, not face further threats to their lives.

\*\*\*

*For more information, please contact: Dan Teng’o, dan.tengo@un.org; +249 91 253 2791*

source.name: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

fields.title: Statement by the United Nations Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in Sudan, Denise Brown
fields.body:
***(Khartoum, 10 October 2026)*** I am horrified by reports of a drone strike next to a displacement site in Wad Al Mahi, Blue Nile State, an area under the control of the Sudanese Armed Forces that has come under attack in the past week. IDPs at the site had been displaced by recent hostilities in Geissan and Kurmuk localities.

Preliminary information indicates that at least 31 civilians have been killed, mostly women and children, and dozens more injured, some seriously. Casualty figures may rise further.

Condemning these senseless killings is essential, but there must also be accountability for this flagrant disregard for international humanitarian law.

A similar senseless attack took place on a displacement shelter in El Obeid in North Kordofan State a week ago, killing and injuring more innocent civilians, including children.

Areas of Blue Nile State have been under continuous attack in recent weeks, displacing thousands of civilians and exposing many more to death, direct harm and further hardship.

As each day goes by in this war, the world continues to accept the suffering of the people of Sudan. International humanitarian law (IHL) is a binding body of law which, when upheld, protects civilians and also the humanitarian and medical personnel serving them. Those who disregard IHL need to be held accountable.

\*\*\*

*For more information, please contact: Dan Teng’o, dan.tengo@un.org; +249 91 253 2791*

source.name: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
UN Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in Sudan

fields.title: Statement by the Humanitarian Coordinator for Somalia, Mr. George Conway, on escalating violence in Baidoa.
fields.body:
*Mogadishu, 9 October 2026* – I am gravely concerned by the escalating violence in Baidoa, South West State, which is taking a heavy toll at a time of exceptionally high humanitarian needs.

The continued insecurity is causing immense suffering among communities already struggling to cope with recurrent shocks and prolonged displacement. I am particularly concerned about people facing heightened risks and vulnerabilities, including internally displaced persons, women, children, older persons and persons with disabilities, who are disproportionately affected by insecurity and repeated displacement.

Repeated outbreaks of violence are compounding the suffering of vulnerable families, forcing people to flee their homes and further undermining their access to safety, essential services and humanitarian assistance. This is especially alarming given the worsening humanitarian situation in Baidoa, where communities face an increased risk of famine, persistently high levels of child malnutrition and a projected risk of El Niño floods.

The protection of civilians must remain paramount. I call on all parties to immediately de-escalate tensions, exercise maximum restraint and take all necessary measures to prevent further violence and protect civilians from harm. All parties must respect their obligations under international humanitarian law and take every possible measure to spare civilians and civilian infrastructure from the effects of hostilities.

Hospitals, health facilities, schools and other civilian infrastructure must be respected and protected at all times. Attacks on medical facilities are prohibited under international humanitarian law. It is equally critical that humanitarian organizations can operate safely and effectively to reach people in need.

I call on all parties to ensure the safety and security of humanitarian personnel and humanitarian assets, and to facilitate safe, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Baidoa. Affected and displaced communities must be able to access life-saving assistance and essential services without discrimination or obstruction.

Humanitarian partners in Somalia are committed to delivering life-saving assistance to the most vulnerable and to working with authorities and communities to prevent further deterioration of the humanitarian situation. However, urgent action is needed to restore calm, prevent further displacement and safeguard civilian lives and dignity.

I urge all parties to take immediate and decisive action to end the violence and prevent further suffering among the people of Baidoa.

End.

source.name: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

fields.title: Ms. Gemma Connell, Director, Crisis Response Division, OCHA, on behalf of Mr. Tom Fletcher, USG for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator – Briefing to the Security Council on the humanitarian situation in Ukraine, 9 October 2026
fields.body:
*As delivered*

Madam President, Excellencies,

The past 48 hours have brought more death and destruction across Ukraine.

Attacks have struck residential areas, public transport and civilian infrastructure across multiple regions.

In the city of Pryluky, residential buildings were hit, killing families, including children. In Kyiv and Kremenchuk, homes and apartment buildings were damaged, while further attacks in Kyiv disrupted electricity and water supplies. And in Kramatorsk, public buses were hit, killing and injuring civilians.

Each attack brings more suffering. Each attack places greater strain on the services civilians depend on.

Madam President,

As winter approaches, repeated attacks on essential infrastructure threaten to turn an already dire situation into something far worse.

Scheduled and emergency power cuts due to attacks on energy infrastructure have already returned, including in Kyiv. As temperatures fall, damage to electricity, heating and water systems will have consequences far beyond the moment of impact.

Local authorities and humanitarian partners are working to restore power and provide generators, materials, cash and emergency assistance. But repeated destruction is making it harder to restore essential services before the next attack.

Preparedness must therefore do two things at once: keep essential services functioning so people can remain safely in their communities, while ensuring that those who choose to leave can do so safely and voluntarily before conditions become critical.

Winter preparedness cannot wait for winter.

Our $358 million Winter Response Plan aims to support more than two million of the most vulnerable people with heating, shelter, food, health care, cash and other essential assistance.

But it only works if resources arrive in time to pre-position supplies, repair homes and heating systems, and help communities withstand the cold before the next disruption becomes a crisis.

Ultimately, no amount of preparedness can substitute for protecting the infrastructure civilians depend upon in the first place.

Madam President,

For some communities, the options are already painfully limited.

Oleshky is one stark example of a wider reality facing civilians in territories of Ukraine occupied by the Russian Federation.

Civilians near front line areas controlled by the Government of Ukraine face similarly severe constraints on movement and access to essential services.

Many remain amid severe insecurity, shortages of food and limited access to medical care. Drone attacks, mines and continuing hostilities make movement, evacuation and the delivery of basic services extremely dangerous.

OCHA has proposed practical solutions to reach these communities.

Humanitarian needs have not diminished.

The urgency has increased.

The parties must agree on practical arrangements for safe and voluntary evacuations and for humanitarian assistance to reach civilians safely and impartially, wherever they are.

OCHA remains ready to support that engagement.

Madam President,

Humanitarian access is not abstract. It depends on humanitarian workers being able to reach people where needs are greatest.

Yesterday, an inter-agency convoy reached Beryslav in Kherson region, where more than 300 civilians remain and access is severely constrained. UN, Red Cross and NGO partners delivered food, medicines and hygiene supplies.

That is what staying and delivering looks like in practice.

Aid workers remain committed to reaching communities close to active hostilities, despite drones, despite shelling, despite mines and despite unsafe roads.

But their courage cannot, and I repeat, cannot become a substitute for their protection.

International humanitarian law is clear: humanitarian personnel must be respected and protected, and parties must allow and facilitate the rapid and unimpeded passage of impartial humanitarian relief for civilians in need.

When humanitarian workers are attacked and when aid movements become too dangerous to deliver aid, civilians pay the price – through delayed assistance, fewer evacuation options and growing isolation.

Madam President,

The way wars are fought is changing. The longstanding rules protecting civilians continue to apply.

Drones and other technologies may alter how attacks are conducted. They do not alter the obligations of the parties to protect civilians and civilian objects, including essential infrastructure on which people depend.

All feasible precautions must be taken to avoid and minimise civilian harm.

Humanitarian personnel and operations must be respected and protected.

Civilian harm is also being reported in the Russian Federation, including damage to infrastructure.

These obligations apply to all parties. Wherever military operations take place, the obligations remain the same.

Madam President,

We must not confuse the ability to adapt with the ability to endure indefinitely.

Aid agencies can change routes. Local authorities can repair infrastructure. Families can ration electricity, move children underground or decide to leave.

But adaptation has limits.

This winter will test more than infrastructure. It will test whether essential civilian systems can continue to function under repeated attack as Ukraine enters a fifth winter of full-scale war.

A family should not have to choose between remaining without heat or water and abandoning its home.

An older person should not be stranded because the road out is too dangerous.

A humanitarian worker should not have to rely on courage to compensate for the absence of protection.

The purpose of humanitarian action is to preserve options for civilians, not to normalise ever-narrower ones.

Madam President,

Three things are needed now.

First, the parties must protect civilians and the infrastructure on which they depend. International humanitarian law applies, whatever the weapon.

Second, we call on the parties to agree on practical arrangements to allow humanitarian aid to reach civilians everywhere, and enable safe and voluntary evacuations wherever needed.

Third, humanitarian personnel must be respected and protected. And when incidents occur, there must be credible investigation and accountability.

Thank you.

source.name: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

fields.title: Mr. Mohamed Yahya, Acting ASG for Humanitarian Affairs, on behalf of Mr. Tom Fletcher, USG for Humanitarian Affairs and Emergency Relief Coordinator – Briefing to the Security Council on the humanitarian situation in Yemen, 9 October 2026
fields.body:
*As delivered*

Madam President,

I thank \[UN\] Special Envoy \[of the Secretary-General Hans\] Grundberg for his briefing and his continued efforts to advance a political solution for Yemen.

Today, I must warn the Council that Yemen’s humanitarian crisis has sharply worsened and further inaction will cost lives.

Over the past two months, escalating fighting has brought renewed suffering to civilians already exhausted by more than a decade of conflict. Families are once again fleeing their homes, with depleted savings, disrupted livelihoods and few options for safety.

More than 200,000 people have been displaced across Yemen since the beginning of August.

This is the highest level of new displacement since the 2022 truce. In addition, nearly 4,000 people have fled across the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to seek safety in Djibouti and Somalia.

Madam President,

Behind every displacement figure is a family facing an impossible choice: stay and risk their lives, or leave and lose everything again.

Women and children are paying the highest price.

Since the start of August, the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights has reported at least 46 civilians have been killed and more than 130 injured.

More than half of those killed and nearly one third of those injured were children.

These figures capture only verified incidents. The full civilian toll is likely higher.

Even before this escalation, 2.2 million children under five were acutely malnourished. And more than half a million were suffering from severe acute malnutrition.

At the same time, nearly 250 schools have closed. And more than 137,000 students are out of the classroom without access to school feeding programs.

Madam President,

The fighting is also pushing Yemen’s health system closer to collapse.

WHO and health partners report only three in five assessed health facilities across the country are fully functioning and few with trauma care.

Conflict-related casualties are placing severe pressure on the health system and limiting other services, including emergency care for women giving birth.

The risk of disease is also rising.

This year, WHO advises that more than 7,800 suspected cholera cases and over 22,000 suspected measles cases have been reported across Yemen. Overcrowded displacement sites, unsafe water and inadequate sanitation are now creating conditions for further outbreaks.

All of this is unfolding amid food insecurity, economic decline, climate shocks and prolonged vulnerability.

Madam President,

Despite these challenges, humanitarian organizations continue to deliver.

Since the beginning of August, the United Nations and our partners have provided emergency assistance to more than 131,000 people affected by the recent escalation. This includes food, shelter, health and protection services.

Health partners have deployed mobile medical systems, activated rapid \[response\] mechanisms and delivered urgent medical supplies.

I pay tribute to all our humanitarian partners, our Yemeni staff and front-line responders. They continue to serve communities under immense pressure.

But the reality is that the humanitarian response in Yemen is falling behind – not because of a lack of effort on the part of those working on the ground, but because of a simple lack of funding.

In direct response to the recent escalation, close to $20 million has been mobilized – nearly $11 million through the Yemen Humanitarian Fund \[YHF\] and another $9 million though the Central Emergency \[Response\] Fund \[CERF\] – to support newly displaced families and communities hosting them.

On top of this, the ERC \[Emergency Relief Coordinator, Tom Fletcher,\] has allocated additional $18 million from the Central Emergency \[Response\] Fund to support life-saving assistance across Yemen.

But the CERF and the YHF funding alone cannot fill the gap.

The humanitarian appeal is only 22 per cent funded. The gap between needs and resources is widening precisely as crisis grows. Aid organizations are already making difficult decisions: which needs to cover and which communities to drop.

The immediate cost of underfunding is clear. Fewer clinics operating. Fewer children receiving nutrition treatment. Fewer families receiving food. Fewer women accessing maternal health care. And ultimately, more preventable deaths.

Without adequate response, the crisis will deepen, and recovery will be harder and more costly. And the ability of families to withstand even small future shocks is eroded, their security under greater threat and chances of building a better future becomes even more remote.

Madam President,

In addition to the lack of funding, the humanitarian operation faces other obstacles.

This month sees continued arbitrary detention of 72 United Nations colleagues and ongoing concerns about the safety of our staff.

The consequences for this are profound. Needs are acute in many areas, while an unsafe operating environment, along with funding shortages, have sharpened and reduced humanitarian reach.

I welcome the release of one United Nations staff member last week. I join the Secretary-General in calling for the release of all detained UN personnel and other humanitarian workers in Yemen.

Madam President,

My appeals are straightforward.

First, all parties must protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, including health facilities and schools. Ambulances and medics must be able to reach and care for the injured and the sick without impediment or harm. There must be adherence to international humanitarian law.

Second, humanitarian access must be safe, rapid and unimpeded. The limited emergency supplies available on the ground must not be delayed or prevented from reaching people in need.

Open the roads. Let humanitarians do their job. And let people receive much needed relief.

Third, donors must urgently unlock flexible and predictable funding. We must respond to new displacements while sustaining life-saving services elsewhere, including through the Yemen Humanitarian Fund.

Finally, efforts on political solutions will be important.

Further fighting will cause further humanitarian consequences. It will displace more people and further restrict humanitarian access.

The people of Yemen need more than our concern and our outrage. They need our collective action, our concrete support and our unwavering commitment to deliver.

I thank you.

source.name: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

fields.title: Renewed hostilities in northern Ethiopia: mixed migration consequences
fields.body:
**Five years after MMC assessed the** [**mixed migration consequences of the Tigray war**](https://mixedmigration.org/articles/mixed-migration-consequences-of-the-tigrayan-crisis/)**, northern Ethiopia is seeing a resurgence of active hostilities. This time the regional alignments are different,** [**the Red Sea is in turmoil**](https://mixedmigration.org/publications/mmr/2026/bab-el-mandeb-yemenis-flee-migrants-arrive/)**, aid budgets have collapsed and drought is setting in. What could this mean for mixed migration and displacement, for the more than one million refugees Ethiopia already hosts and for Ethiopians on the move?**

## **Back to hostilities, but with different players**

In January 2021, a few months into the previous war in Tigray, we [**looked at the likely mixed migration consequences**](https://mixedmigration.org/articles/mixed-migration-consequences-of-the-tigrayan-crisis/) of that crisis. Our main conclusion was that mass internal displacement and involuntary immobility, rather than large-scale cross-border movement, would be the most likely and most numerous outcomes. That turned out to be largely right. With the recent resurgence of clashes, it is worth asking the same questions again now.

The renewed fighting builds on years of instability. Amhara has seen [**armed violence between federal forces and Fano militias**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/brf/africa/horn-africa/ethiopia/b194-ethiopias-ominous-new-war-amhara) since 2023, when the government also declared a [**state of emergency**](https://acleddata.com/brief/fact-sheet-crisis-ethiopias-amhara-region) in the region. In Tigray, [**recovery since the 2022 cessation of hostilities agreement has been slow**](https://riftvalley.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/RVI-20260326-Tigray-CTA-PRF-Final.pdf), with limited reconstruction and very high unemployment, especially among demobilised youth.

After months of rising tension and [**clashes**](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/3/tigray-refugees-flee-into-sudan-after-deadly-violence-on-ethiopia-border) near the [**Sudanese border**](https://sudantribune.com/article/316940) in early August 2026, armed opposition groups in Tigray, Amhara and Afar [**formed an alliance and launched an offensive on 23 September**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/stm/africa/ethiopia-eritrea/arresting-dangerous-descent-back-war-northern-ethiopia). Fighting has since [**spread**](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/2/how-the-fighting-in-ethiopia-spread-beyond-tigray-in-maps-and-charts) along the Tigray–Amhara and Tigray–Afar boundaries, and towns have changed hands in [**both directions**](https://www.criticalthreats.org/briefs/ethiopia-war-security-review/ethiopia-war-security-review-september-29-2026). On 1 October, Ethiopia closed its embassy in Asmara and expelled Eritrean diplomats, and Eritrea [**cut diplomatic ties**](https://www.dawan.africa/news/eritrea-severs-diplomatic-ties-with-ethiopia-after-embassy-closure).

The key difference with 2020/21 is Eritrea’s position. Then, Eritrean forces fought alongside the Ethiopian federal army in Tigray. Now, according to the [**International Crisis Group**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/stm/africa/ethiopia-eritrea/arresting-dangerous-descent-back-war-northern-ethiopia), Eritrea is “quietly aligned with its former enemy” in Tigray. The Ethiopian government accuses Eritrea, as well as Sudan and Egypt, of backing the armed opposition groups. [**All three deny this**](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/29/ethiopia-blames-regional-rivals-as-risk-of-conflict-spillover-rises). How does this changed situation affect people on the move?

## **A region where every crisis touches the next**

This is not only an Ethiopian crisis. As Crisis Group’s Alan Boswell [**wrote in July**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/cmt/africa/horn-africa/horn-africa-nears-boiling-point-time-urgent-diplomacy), “the Horn of Africa is combustible”. He [**describes**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/cmt/africa/horn-africa/horn-africa-nears-boiling-point-time-urgent-diplomacy) two loose blocs forming around the war in Sudan, with Eritrea, Egypt, Djibouti and Somalia, among others, on one side, and Ethiopia among those aligned with the United Arab Emirates on the other. Sudan’s war is the main destabiliser, and the risk is “a belt of interconnected wars stretching from Yemen in the east to Chad in the west”. Ethiopia and Sudan’s army-led government accuse each other of supporting each other’s armed opponents, and [**Crisis Group**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/stm/africa/ethiopia-eritrea/arresting-dangerous-descent-back-war-northern-ethiopia) warns of the risk that the two wars merge.

Then there is the sea. Ethiopia, a country of some 120 million people, is landlocked and depends on Djibouti for [**around 90% of its trade**](https://africacenter.org/spotlight/2026-houthi-red-sea-threats/). Access to the sea, and specifically the Eritrean port of Assab, has been an openly stated government [**ambition**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/cmt/africa/horn-africa/horn-africa-nears-boiling-point-time-urgent-diplomacy), and Eritrea regards access to it from Ethiopia as a red line. This dispute over sea access has been one of the main drivers of [**deteriorating relations**](https://www.chathamhouse.org/2025/11/de-escalation-needed-prevent-ethiopia-and-eritrea-going-war) between the two countries in recent years, so the closure of the Ethiopian embassy in Asmara did not come out of the blue. Since the [**change in territorial control of Yemen’s west coast and the Bab el-Mandeb**](https://mixedmigration.org/publications/mmr/2026/bab-el-mandeb-yemenis-flee-migrants-arrive/) strait in September, weekly transits through the strait have fallen to around 25 vessels, compared with around 80 before October 2023. Ethiopia has [**seen**](https://africacenter.org/spotlight/2026-houthi-red-sea-threats/) fuel prices rise by 63% since April, while food prices in Sudan have risen by around 40%. Some of the fighting in Afar came close to the [**road between Addis Ababa and Djibouti**](https://www.criticalthreats.org/briefs/ethiopia-war-security-review/ethiopia-war-security-review-september-29-2026), Ethiopia’s economic lifeline.

## **Polycrisis, not just fighting**

The resurgence of war is happening on top of other shocks. A [**July analysis**](https://theconversation.com/africas-greater-horn-region-is-facing-a-looming-polycrisis-fueled-by-conflict-prices-climate-and-disease-286071) in The Conversation warned of a “major, multicountry polycrisis” in the Greater Horn: a strengthening El Niño and failed rains, higher food and fertiliser prices because of the war in Iran, conflict in almost every country of the region, and a “devastating aid cliff”. These shocks, they argue, “are not simply additive but multiplicative”.

Meanwhile, UNHCR’s Ethiopia operation was [**25% funded**](https://www.unhcr.org/media/ethiopia-funding-update-2026) at the end of September. Since late 2025, around 800,000 refugees in Ethiopia have been receiving [**40% food rations**](https://www.thereporterethiopia.com/47375/), under 1,000 calories a day.

## **What could it mean for mixed migration?**

As in 2021, it helps to look at the different groups affected by the current resurgence of hostilities, because the consequences will be different for each.

### **Internal displacement and involuntary immobility**

Ethiopia already had [**around 1.9 million IDPs**](https://data.unhcr.org/en/documents/details/124293) before this escalation, including some 750,000 in Tigray who were never able to return after the 2022 Ethiopia-Tigray cessation of hostilities agreement (the Pretoria agreement). Due to this new outbreak of violence, [**local organisations estimate**](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/29/fighting-in-ethiopia-intensifies-whats-the-latest) that around 150,000 people have been displaced in Afar alone in recent weeks, although no UN figure is available yet and humanitarian access is severely restricted. As in 2020/21, internal displacement is likely to be the largest consequence of this war by far. And for many, the outcome will be no movement at all. People without money, with closed roads and front lines all around them, and with aid unable to reach them, become involuntarily immobile, trapped in dire situations. They are the least visible and often the most vulnerable.

### **Refugees already in Ethiopia**

Ethiopia hosts [**1,129,183 refugees and asylum-seekers**](https://data.unhcr.org/en/country/eth), mainly from South Sudan, Somalia, Eritrea and Sudan. For Eritreans, [**some 170,000 people**](https://data.unhcr.org/en/documents/details/124293), the change in regional alignments is particularly worrying. Several of their camps, in Afar (Asayita, Berhale) and in Amhara (Alemwach), are [**in or close to the areas now affected**](https://mixedmigration.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/379-Where-to-Next-Eritrean-displacement.pdf). In 2020/21, Eritrean refugees in Tigray were caught between the warring parties, and two camps, Hitsats and Shimelba, were destroyed. This time, with Ethiopia and Eritrea openly hostile, the risk is that Eritrean refugees face suspicion because of their nationality. Human Rights Concern-Eritrea has [**warned**](https://martinplaut.com/2026/10/02/escalating-ethiopia-eritrea-tensions-place-eritrean-refugees-and-civilians-at-grave-risk/) of risks of arbitrary detention, forced recruitment, trafficking and forced return.

Meanwhile, Sudanese refugees, [**some 101,000**](https://data.unhcr.org/en/documents/details/124293), fled one war only to find themselves next to another, while still [**waiting for registration**](https://reliefweb.int/report/ethiopia/ethiopia-sudanese-asylum-seekers-fleeing-ethiopia-dg-echo-media-dg-echo-partners-echo-daily-flash-9-february-2026) in some locations. This is not new for them. In 2024, thousands of Sudanese refugees [**fled the Kumer and Awlala camps in Amhara**](https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/news-feature/2024/06/27/sudan-refugees-trapped-ethiopia-forest-call-immediate-evacuation) after attacks by militias and bandits, and many ended up stranded in a nearby forest. The ongoing violence makes an already insecure situation worse. For both groups of refugees, if caught up in the conflict, the options are likely to be limited, ranging from staying where they are, further displacement within Ethiopia or – likely to a limited extent – seeking safety in other neighbouring countries.

The fighting also comes at a delicate moment for refugee policy. In June 2026, Ethiopia launched the [**Makatet Roadmap**](https://ethiopia.un.org/en/317669-ethiopia-launches-groundbreaking-makatet-roadmap-ushering-era-refugee-inclusion), an ambitious ten-year plan to move from camps towards integrated settlements, giving refugees access to work and national services alongside host communities. Renewed hostilities, economic strain and pressure on public budgets could make it harder to implement. It will be important that these commitments are not rolled back in the face of greater internal challenges.

### **Eritreans in Eritrea and on the move**

Eritrea is preparing for possible escalation. In February 2025, the government [**called up reserves**](https://borkena.com/2025/02/21/eritrea-mobilizes-military-reserves-imposes-travel-restrictions-amid-rising-tensions-with-ethiopia/) and reportedly restricted people under 50 from leaving the country. Indefinite national service has long been the [main reason](https://mixedmigration.org/4mi-data-explorer/en) Eritreans leave, and a new war will add to that. But the routes out of Eritrea are narrowing. The traditional first countries of refuge, Ethiopia and Sudan, are both insecure, and the border with Ethiopia might once again become a front line. This is likely to mean fewer, more dangerous and more expensive departures, with more reliance on smugglers, rather than a large and visible outflow. While back in 2016, Eritreans were among the top nationalities of arrival in Italy, their arrivals have since dropped to relatively low numbers. As of the end of August, arrivals of Eritreans in Italy stood at [**1,185**](https://data.unhcr.org/en/situations/mediterranean/location/5205), and it is unlikely these numbers will suddenly rise again because of the current hostilities.

### **Ethiopians seeking refuge across borders**

In 2020-21, more than 60,000 Ethiopians fled to Sudan. Sudan still hosts [**around 63,000 Ethiopian refugees**](https://data.unhcr.org/en/country/sdn?_gl=1*p61vze*_gcl_au*MTg0OTI0MDUyLjE3ODg5NDM0MzUuLS4tLjE3ODg5NDM0NDUuMTIyMjA5NDEwMS4xNzkxMjgyNTE2LjE3OTEyODQwODY.*_rup_ga*Mjc5NTY3MDM1LjE3ODgyNzE3NTE.*_rup_ga_EVDQTJ4LMY*czE3OTEyODI0NDUkbzEwJGcxJHQxNzkxMjg0MDc2JGozJGwwJGgw*_fplc*NmxjVUM1OHlLdG45TVQzUUtvNW9IdWolMkJrNjRrZkE3d0s4NW1QJTJGWTVOT0ltRVRWWDF1bHJrM3hoZW43MjNzd2tDbTdXTmhTN0E3dTNObllUakklMkJINWlrNTVtbUZJJTJGcVRwSHlnTVg2OXBhUkppRkV4UGtmTSUyRjF1R3o3VzhqZyUzRCUzRA..*_ga*Mjc5NTY3MDM1LjE3ODgyNzE3NTE.*_ga_X2YZPJ1XWR*czE3OTEyODI1MDUkbzQkZzEkdDE3OTEyODQwNzYkajYwJGwwJGgxODg2NDgyNTcy), and in August, camps near the border were [**hit during fighting**](https://sudantribune.com/article/316940) on the Ethiopian side. With Sudan itself at war, it is no longer an obvious place of safety. Djibouti is the other neighbour within reach of Afar. It is a small country that is now already receiving [**thousands of Yemenis**](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/22/un-warns-of-rising-yemen-displacement-as-thousands-flee-to-djibouti) fleeing across the Bab el-Mandeb as a result of [**recent fighting and shifts in territorial control**](https://mixedmigration.org/publications/mmr/2026/bab-el-mandeb-yemenis-flee-migrants-arrive/) along Yemen’s west coast, with a UNHCR operation [**only 27% funded**](https://www.unhcr.org/sites/default/files/docs/default/2026-10/djibouti-funding-30-09-2026.pdf). So far, there are no reports of significant refugee arrivals from Ethiopia in Djibouti, Kenya or Somaliland. But if the fighting in Afar intensifies, Djibouti could face pressure from both sides at once and will struggle to cope.

### **The Eastern route**

The so-called Eastern route out of the Horn of Africa towards Yemen and onward to Saudi Arabia, is where the new conflict potentially links to one of the largest irregular migration corridors out of Africa. In the first quarter of 2026, IOM found that [**35% of Ethiopians on the Eastern Route came from Amhara and another 35% from Tigray**](https://reliefweb.int/report/ethiopia/migration-along-eastern-route-report-63-january-march-2026-publication-12-august-2026), with 22% from Oromia. In other words, around 70% came from the two regions now most affected by the fighting. In 2026, the route has already been [**busier than ever**](https://mixedmigration.org/publications/mmr/2026/bab-el-mandeb-yemenis-flee-migrants-arrive/), with 122,258 arrivals in Yemen between January and August 2026. Most people (88%) [say they leave](https://mixedmigration.org/4mi-data-explorer/en) for economic reasons. About a fifth cite conflict directly. But the fighting might deepen those economic pressures or add conflict as an additional driver.

So, could we expect more people on the Eastern route? It is plausible, but not certain. To reach Djibouti, many Ethiopians transit through Afar, where the situation remains volatile, and the onward journey leads into a Yemen where the coast has just changed hands (even though this may rapidly change again). Two things could happen at once: more people wanting to leave, and fewer able to do so safely. That could mean shifting routes, towards Somaliland and Puntland to cross the Gulf of Aden from there, higher smuggling fees and more risks.

## **Looking ahead**

Five years ago, we concluded that most consequences of the Tigray war would be internal and regional, not a large movement out of the region, let alone towards Europe. That is likely to be true again. But the context is much harsher. The neighbouring countries are themselves at war or under strain, the Red Sea is a conflict zone, drought is setting in, and the humanitarian system has far less capacity than it had in 2020.

That means the main concern should not be how many people might move onwards, but the protection of those who are already displaced, stranded or trapped. That includes Ethiopians caught near the front lines, refugees in Ethiopia, and Eritrean refugees in particular, who now find themselves in a country potentially at war with a government they fled. As [**Crisis Group**](https://www.crisisgroup.org/stm/africa/ethiopia-eritrea/arresting-dangerous-descent-back-war-northern-ethiopia) puts it, “it is not too late to avert a return to costly, bloody war”. For the people on the move in this region, much depends on whether that happens.

### **Bram Frouws**

**Author** Bram Frouws is the Director of the Mixed Migration Centre (MMC) and a migration researcher with extensive experience across Africa, Asia, and Europe. He writes widely on migration and displacement. Bram tweets from [**@bramfrouws**](https://x.com/BramFrouws)

fields.title: UN Women statement for the International Day of the Girl 2026
fields.body:
Globally, [one in five girls is married before the age of 18](https://www.unicef.org/gender-equality/international-day-girl). Every year, [more than 12 million](https://www.un.org/en/observances/girl-child-day) girls are married in childhood, roughly one every three seconds. Behind every statistic is a girl whose education, health, safety, choices, and future are put at risk.

Child marriage is preventable. And progress is possible. Over the past 25 years, investments in girls’ education, legal reform, and social protection have helped avert an estimated [68 million child marriages](https://www.un.org/en/observances/girl-child-day).

We know what works. What is needed now is the political will and sustained investment to reach every girl.

Investing in girls means more than protecting them from harm. It means keeping girls in school. Ensuring access to health, protection, and social services. Strengthening their voice and leadership. And supporting families and communities to stand behind girls’ choices.

On [International Day of the Girl](https://www.un.org/en/observances/girl-child-day) (11 October), we call on governments, partners, civil society, communities, and the private sector to turn commitments into action: enforce laws that protect girls; keep girls in school; expand access to essential services; challenge harmful norms; fund girl-led and women-led organizations; and ensure that solutions reach the girls most at risk, including those affected by poverty, conflict, displacement, disability, and crisis.

Invest in girls’ rights. End child marriage. Give every girl the freedom to choose her future.

fields.title: Safe and dignified burials help prevent the spread of Ebola
fields.body:
**Bunia, Democratic Republic of the Congo**—In Ituri Province, in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, safe and dignified burials play a critical role in the fight against Ebola. The disease spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person, and after death, certain burial practices can expose family members to the virus if appropriate protective measures are not in place. In a region where funeral rites are central to community life, protecting families while respecting traditions remains essential.

When the current outbreak began in the province, health teams were met with considerable mistrust in some communities. “In the beginning, many people did not understand why health teams needed to intervene during burials,” explains Pastor Richard Ndjaridjo. Some families hesitated to report deaths and continued to organize funerals on their own. In some cases, bodies that had already been buried were exhumed to allow relatives to carry out certain traditional rites. Teams responsible for safe and dignified burials also faced threats and attacks, complicating efforts to stop the spread of the virus. In this context, developing an approach that protected communities while respecting their beliefs and cultural practices became a priority.

To address these challenges, the Ministry of Health, with support from the World Health Organization (WHO) and partners, implemented a community engagement approach. Through the Standby Partners mechanism, Paul Benjamin Gbadia was deployed to WHO to support the Ebola response in Ituri. Faced with the difficulties encountered by safe and dignified burials teams during the early stages of the outbreak, he helped strengthen an approach that placed communities at the centre of the response. Working alongside health authorities and partners, he helped train and mentor local volunteers so they could participate directly in safe and dignified burial activities.

“We found that communities were more willing to accept safe and dignified burials when they were directly involved in the response,” he explains. “By engaging local volunteers, we were able to establish closer dialogue with families and better address their concerns.”

In Jina, in Djugu Territory, 36 community members were trained and assigned to safe and dignified burial and decontamination teams. Comprised of people known and trusted by residents, these teams support families while applying the measures needed to prevent Ebola transmission. For Paul, the goal was to make communities active participants in the response rather than passive beneficiaries. “Local volunteers speak the language, understand the customs and know the concerns of their communities. This closeness makes dialogue easier and helps build acceptance of prevention measures,” says Gbadia.

Over time, this approach helped strengthen trust between communities and health teams. Recalling a recent death in Jina, Naema Mave, a member of a safe and dignified burial team, describes how the family immediately alerted health authorities and waited for the team to arrive before proceeding with the burial. “When we arrived, no one had touched the body. A few months earlier, that might not have been the case,” she explains.

For Mave, this progress reflects the value of the training and support provided to local volunteers, enabling them to respond safely and independently within their communities.

Ndjaridjo also attributes this change to sustained community awareness efforts. “There has been a lot of sensitization. People have come to understand that bodies can transmit the disease and they now accept the intervention of safe and dignified burial teams to protect families,” he says.

Beyond training community teams, WHO has provided technical, logistical and operational support to safe and dignified burial activities. This support includes personal protective equipment, essential operational supplies, transportation to reach remote areas and ongoing field mentoring for teams.

Since the start of the response, and as of 27 September 2026, more than 11 573 alerts have been recorded, 10 357 safe and dignified burials conducted in Ituri and 9 433 laboratory samples collected and tested. Twenty safe and dignified burial teams, including 10 mobile teams and 10 community-based teams, have received operational, logistical and training support. These results highlight the importance of a trust-based approach.

“When communities participate directly in safe and dignified burial activities, they take greater ownership of prevention measures. This has helped reduce resistance and better protect families,” says Gbadia.

According to Dr Danny Byaruhanga, Medical Director of Jina, community involvement has strengthened the response. “We can say that safe and dignified burial teams have played a major role in interrupting transmission within the community. Once families accepted that burials could be carried out by trained and properly equipped personnel, it significantly reduced the risks associated with handling bodies,” he explains.

Beyond its immediate impact on preventing Ebola transmission, this approach is also helping communities build their capacity to respond to future public health emergencies. By encouraging participation and ownership of prevention activities, it promotes the adoption of protective practices and behaviours that can continue long after the current outbreak has ended.

In Ituri, experience has shown that safe and dignified burials rely as much on trust as on protective measures. When a family reports a death, accepts support from a trained team and takes part in prevention efforts, a high-risk situation can become an opportunity to protect an entire community.

fields.title: Ghana strengthens national ownership of vaccine decisions
fields.body:
Ghana is strengthening how it decides which vaccines to introduce, replace, reschedule or defer as the country works to protect immunization gains and build a more sustainable national programme.

The Expanded Programme on Immunization has contributed significantly to reducing illness, disability and deaths from vaccine-preventable diseases. However, the growing number of available vaccines, changing disease patterns, rising programme costs and reductions in external financing have made vaccine policy decisions more complex.

The question is no longer simply which vaccine Ghana should introduce next. The country must also consider which interventions will deliver the greatest public-health benefit, how they fit within the health system and whether they can be sustainably financed without affecting coverage, equity or quality.

The Ministry of Health, Ghana Health Service and National Immunization Technical Advisory Group of Ghana (NITAG-Ghana) are therefore using a structured Vaccine Prioritization and Optimization (VPOP) exercise, with technical support from the World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF.

The exercise marks a shift from considering vaccine proposals individually to looking at Ghana’s immunization portfolio as a whole.

Ghana is considering several vaccines and interventions in response to current and emerging public-health needs, including the hepatitis B birth dose, rabies vaccine, typhoid conjugate vaccine, oral cholera vaccine and interventions against respiratory syncytial virus. The country is also assessing whether changes to existing vaccines, products and schedules could improve health impact, simplify service delivery or make the programme more sustainable.

Each option has potential benefits, costs and implementation implications. Introducing a new vaccine or changing a schedule can affect procurement, cold-chain capacity, vaccine supply, health-worker workload, logistics, surveillance and the number of visits required to vaccinate a child.

WHO Ghana supported the Government of Ghana and NITAG-Ghana to establish a transparent and evidence-informed approach to assessing these options.

The support included helping national experts define the policy questions, review available evidence and adapt global guidance to Ghana’s disease burden, economic context and programme realities. Structured Evidence-to-Decision frameworks were developed to assess factors including public-health benefits, risks, costs, equity, acceptability, feasibility, vaccine availability, cold-chain requirements, health-worker workload and long-term financing.

WHO also supported technical working sessions involving NITAG-Ghana members, the National Immunization Programme and other national experts. Participants reviewed the evidence, considered the benefits and trade-offs of different options and developed recommendations for national consideration.

UNICEF complemented the process with expertise in vaccine procurement, supply systems and market considerations, while ensuring that the exercise remained nationally led and reflected Ghana’s priorities.

Importantly, the process does not assume that every beneficial vaccine or intervention should become an immediate priority. Instead, it helps distinguish between options that should be prioritized now, those that could proceed under defined conditions, those requiring further planning and those that may need to be deferred.

This approach enables Ghana to consider the wider implications of each decision and make better use of limited resources, particularly as the country prepares for changes in external financing.

It also strengthens national ownership. Recommendations are developed through Ghana’s established advisory structures and informed by local evidence and programme realities. WHO provides technical guidance and global evidence, while national institutions determine the country’s priorities and policy direction.

The exercise further provides a clearer basis for Ghana’s engagement with Gavi and other partners. Rather than responding to vaccine opportunities individually, the country can present a nationally considered portfolio based on disease burden, health impact, equity, feasibility and long-term sustainability.

The value of the VPOP process therefore goes beyond individual vaccine recommendations. It strengthens the system Ghana uses to make vaccine policy decisions and helps ensure that choices made today can be implemented and sustained over time.

The next steps are to finalize the Vaccine Prioritization and Optimization report, use its findings to inform updates to the National Immunization Strategy and prepare Ghana’s application for Gavi support.

Through VPOP, Ghana is strengthening a nationally led approach to vaccine decision-making that brings evidence, public-health priorities and long-term sustainability together.

fields.title: ACNUR pide inversiones urgentes ante el agravamiento de la crisis de desplazamiento en el Sahel Central
fields.body:
*Este texto resume las declaraciones de Abdouraouf Gnon-Konde, Director de la Oficina Regional de ACNUR para África Occidental y Central -a quien pueden atribuirse las citas textuales-, durante la rueda de prensa celebrada en el Palacio de las Naciones, en Ginebra.*

GINEBRA – ACNUR, la Agencia de la ONU para los Refugiados, alerta del agravamiento de la crisis de desplazamiento en el Sahel Central, donde cerca de cuatro millones de personas se han visto obligadas a abandonar sus hogares en Burkina Faso, Malí y Níger. Entre ellas más de 818.000 refugiados y solicitantes de asilo. La cifra prácticamente duplica la registrada en octubre de 2020, cuando la región contabilizaba más de 1,7 millones de desplazados internos y 365.000 refugiados.

La crisis se ve agravada por los continuos ataques que afectan a la población civil, los fenómenos climáticos extremos y la grave falta de financiación humanitaria. La combinación de estos factores obliga a más familias a huir, socava sus medios de vida y limita las posibilidades de las personas desplazadas de reconstruir sus vidas, lo que provoca nuevos desplazamientos tanto dentro de la región como fuera de ella.

En Malí, la inmensa mayoría de los refugiados procede del vecino Burkina Faso. En Koro, en la región de Bandiagara, unos 86.000 refugiados burkineses habían encontrado refugio hasta julio de 2026, tras sucesivas oleadas de desplazamiento iniciadas en 2025. Entre ellos figuran más de 14.000 niños y 6.000 mujeres identificados como especialmente vulnerables. La población refugiada se acerca ya en número a la comunidad de acogida, lo que aumenta la presión sobre unos recursos de tierra y agua ya escasos, unos servicios sanitarios desbordados y unas oportunidades de subsistencia limitadas.

Los fenómenos climáticos extremos añaden presión a unas comunidades que ya afrontan el desplazamiento y la inseguridad. Las sequías recurrentes, las lluvias irregulares y las inundaciones alteran la producción agrícola, dañan viviendas e infraestructuras y dificultan el acceso al agua y a los medios de vida. Para las familias que dependen en gran medida de la agricultura y la ganadería, estos fenómenos merman aún más su capacidad para subsistir.

Mientras se buscan soluciones políticas a largo plazo, es necesario reforzar de inmediato y de forma sustancial el apoyo a los refugiados, los desplazados internos y las comunidades que los acogen. Urgen más recursos para proteger a las personas más vulnerables, garantizar el acceso a los servicios básicos, incluida la educación, y ampliar las oportunidades de subsistencia. Todo ello se enmarca en la [visión 50 by 35](https://www.unhcr.org/50-by-35) de ACNUR, cuyo objetivo es promover la autosuficiencia y encontrar soluciones duraderas de aquí a 2035 para los refugiados en situación de desplazamiento prolongado.

En Koro, varias iniciativas de cooperativas agrícolas que reúnen a refugiados burkineses y miembros de las comunidades de acogida han permitido ampliar la superficie cultivada de 21 hectáreas en 2025 a 45 en 2026, con la consiguiente mejora de la producción de alimentos y de los ingresos familiares. En Kaya, en Burkina Faso, proyectos similares ayudan a los desplazados internos y a las comunidades de acogida a aumentar la producción de alimentos, reducir las pérdidas postcosecha y generar ingresos.

Estas iniciativas siguen siendo modestas frente a la magnitud de los desplazamientos, pero demuestran lo que puede lograrse cuando las personas obligadas a huir disponen de los medios necesarios para reconstruir sus vidas mientras se buscan soluciones a largo plazo. Para ampliar estos proyectos será necesario mantener la inversión, reforzar los sistemas nacionales, crear más oportunidades de subsistencia y apoyar tanto a la población desplazada como a las comunidades de acogida.

La crisis, además, se extiende cada vez más allá del Sahel Central. En 2026, casi 500.000 refugiados y solicitantes de asilo burkineses habían buscado protección en países vecinos, frente a los más de 300.000 registrados a finales de 2025. Muchos han huido a países costeros de África Occidental, entre ellos Benín, Costa de Marfil, Ghana y Togo. Más de 334.000 malienses viven asimismo como refugiados en otros países, mientras que más de 106.000 nigerinos figuran registrados como refugiados y solicitantes de asilo en Estados vecinos.

Para algunas personas, el desplazamiento no termina al llegar a un país vecino. Cuando no encuentran seguridad ni perspectivas de futuro, los refugiados pueden continuar su viaje, a menudo junto a migrantes, por rutas peligrosas hacia el norte de África y Europa. Esta situación pone de relieve las repercusiones regionales e internacionales de la inseguridad prolongada y de la falta de oportunidades en los países de origen y su entorno.

Para reforzar la protección y ofrecer soluciones a refugiados y migrantes a lo largo de las principales rutas de la región, ACNUR trabaja con gobiernos y organizaciones socias en la creación de centros de servicios polivalentes. Estos centros proporcionan información esencial, asesoramiento, derivación a otros servicios y asistencia básica.

Al mismo tiempo, la grave falta de financiación está debilitando la respuesta humanitaria justo cuando las necesidades no dejan de aumentar. En septiembre de 2026, la respuesta de ACNUR en el Sahel solo había recibido el 27% de los 329,6 millones de dólares necesarios, lo que obliga a tomar decisiones difíciles sobre qué servicios y actividades esenciales pueden mantenerse.

La falta de fondos afecta a labores fundamentales de protección y asistencia, como el registro y la documentación, el alojamiento, el acceso a los servicios básicos y el apoyo a los medios de vida. Las consecuencias van más allá de las necesidades humanitarias inmediatas. Sin asistencia suficiente ni oportunidades para alcanzar la autosuficiencia, refugiados y desplazados internos tienen cada vez más dificultades para rehacer sus vidas, mientras que las comunidades de acogida disponen de menos recursos para atender a una población creciente.

Con cerca de cuatro millones de personas desplazadas, ha llegado el momento de redoblar los esfuerzos, no de dar un paso atrás. Los Gobiernos, los socios para el desarrollo, las instituciones financieras internacionales y el sector privado deben invertir desde ahora en protección, servicios, medios de vida y comunidades de acogida, al tiempo que mantienen el compromiso político necesario para abordar la inseguridad que provoca los desplazamientos.

**Para más información, por favor, contacta con:**  
En Dakar (regional), Senan Rose Fidelia Bohissou: bohissou@unhcr.org, +221 77 569 91 60  
En Ginebra, Eujin Byun: byun@unhcr.org, +41 79 747 8719

fields.title: European Union supports Tearfund Netherlands in responding to impact of conflict in the Central African Republic
fields.body:
Utrecht, 9th of October 2026 – Communities in the Lim-Pendé prefecture in the North-West of the Central African Republic (CAR) continue to face the consequences of years of conflict, displacement and underinvestment in basic services. Many schools lack adequate classrooms, safe water and sanitation facilities, while vulnerable families struggle to access essential services. Through European Union humanitarian funding, Tearfund Netherlands is helping to improve access to clean water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services, while supporting safe and inclusive learning environments for children in conflict-affected communities.

 The response forms part of a wider humanitarian programme led by Plan International in Lim-Pendé prefecture. Within this programme, Tearfund is responsible for delivering WASH activities in partnership with the local organisation RHIBES. The intervention will improve access to safe drinking water, sanitation facilities and hygiene promotion for approximately 12,000 people across some of the most vulnerable communities in the sub-prefecture of Ndim.

 ‘The European Union remains committed to supporting people affected by humanitarian crises in the Central African Republic, where conflict and displacement continue to undermine access to essential services, including education, water and sanitation,’ said Jean-Paul Jemmy Ghomsi, Head of the EU Humanitarian Aid office in Bangui. ‘Through our humanitarian funding, we help ensure that vulnerable communities can access safe drinking water, hygiene services and quality education, while strengthening their resilience and protecting their dignity.’

 Needs assessments conducted in the target area revealed severe gaps in basic WASH services. Many communities rely on unsafe water sources, a large number of boreholes are non-functional, and sanitation facilities are either absent or inadequate. Schools are particularly affected, with limited access to water points and hygienic latrines, creating additional barriers to education, especially for girls and children with disabilities.

 Under the project, Tearfund will construct and rehabilitate 17 water points, including solar-powered systems and hand-pump boreholes, improve sanitation facilities in schools and communities, establish water management committees, and promote sustainable hygiene practices through community-led awareness activities. The programme is designed to ensure long-term community ownership and maintenance of the infrastructure.

 ‘Access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene is fundamental for health, protection and education,’ said Martin Herlaar, Director International Programs of Tearfund Netherlands. ‘With support from the European Union, Tearfund is working alongside communities and local partners to restore essential services and help create a safer and healthier environment for children and families affected by conflict.’

 The EU-funded programme is expected to reach more than 22,000 people through integrated education, child protection and WASH interventions. By combining improvements in school infrastructure, access to education, child protection measures and safe water services, the action aims to strengthen the resilience of communities and improve opportunities for children living in one of the country's most vulnerable regions.

 **About Tearfund Netherlands**

 Tearfund Netherlands is part of the global Tearfund family. Together, we work with local partners to tackle poverty, respond to disasters and challenge injustice in more than 50 countries worldwide. Through locally led approaches, Tearfund supports communities affected by conflict, climate change and vulnerability to build resilient and sustainable futures.

 For more information, please contact info@tearfund.nl.

 **About EU Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid**

 The European Union and its Member States are the world's leading donor of humanitarian aid.

 Relief assistance is an expression of European solidarity with people in need all around the world. It aims to save lives, prevent and alleviate human suffering, and safeguard the integrity and human dignity of populations affected by natural disasters and man-made crises.

 Through its Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations DG ECHO, the European Union helps millions of victims of conflict and disasters every year. With headquarters in Brussels and a global network of field offices, the EU provides assistance to the most vulnerable people on the basis of humanitarian needs.

 For more information, please contact Anouk.Delafortrie@echofield.eu.

fields.title: Le HCR appelle à des investissements urgents face à l’aggravation de la crise des déplacements au Sahel central
fields.body:
*Ceci est un résumé des propos tenus par Abdouraouf Gnon-Konde, directeur du Bureau régional du HCR pour l’Afrique de l’Ouest et l’Afrique centrale – à qui toute citation peut être attribuée – lors du point de presse de ce jour, au Palais des Nations à Genève.*

GENÈVE – Le HCR, l'Agence des Nations Unies pour les réfugiés, est toujours plus préoccupé par l'aggravation de la crise des déplacements au Sahel central : près de 4 millions de personnes, dont plus de 818 000 réfugiés et demandeurs d'asile, ont été déracinées au Burkina Faso, au Mali et au Niger. Ce chiffre représente environ le double de celui enregistré en octobre 2020, lorsque la région comptait plus de 1,7 million de personnes déplacées à l’intérieur de leur pays et 365 000 réfugiés.

La crise est exacerbée par la poursuite des attaques qui touchent les populations civiles, les chocs liés au climat et les graves déficits de financement de l’aide humanitaire. Ces pressions conjuguées contraignent un nombre croissant de familles à fuir, fragilisent les moyens de subsistance et limitent les possibilités pour les personnes déplacées de reconstruire leur vie, contribuant à de nouveaux mouvements à l’intérieur de la région et au-delà.

Au Mali, la grande majorité des réfugiés sont originaires du Burkina Faso voisin. À Koro, dans la région de Bandiagara, quelque 86 000 réfugiés burkinabè avaient trouvé refuge en juillet 2026, à la suite de vagues successives de déplacements depuis 2025. Parmi eux figurent plus de 14 000 enfants et 6 000 femmes identifiés comme particulièrement exposés à des risques. Les réfugiés sont désormais presque aussi nombreux que les membres de la communauté d'accueil locale, exerçant une pression croissante sur des terres et des ressources en eau déjà limitées, des services de santé saturés et des moyens de subsistance limités.

Les chocs liés au climat pèsent davantage encore sur des communautés déjà confrontées aux déplacements et à l’insécurité. Les sécheresses récurrentes, l’irrégularité des précipitations et les inondations perturbent la production agricole, endommagent les habitations et les infrastructures et réduisent l’accès à l’eau et aux moyens de subsistance. Pour les familles qui dépendent largement de l’agriculture et de l’élevage, ces phénomènes compromettent davantage leur capacité à subvenir à leurs besoins.

Tandis que des solutions politiques à plus long terme sont recherchées, un soutien bien plus important est nécessaire dès aujourd'hui pour les réfugiés, les personnes déplacées à l'intérieur de leur pays et les communautés qui les accueillent. Des ressources supplémentaires doivent être mobilisées de toute urgence pour protéger les personnes les plus exposées, préserver l'accès aux services essentiels, notamment à l'éducation, et développer les moyens de subsistance, conformément à la vision « 50 by 35 » du HCR, qui vise à renforcer l’autonomie des réfugiés en situation de déplacement prolongé et à faire progresser les solutions durables d’ici à 2035.

À Koro, des initiatives de coopératives agricoles réunissant des réfugiés burkinabè et des membres des communautés d’accueil ont permis de faire passer la superficie des terres cultivées de 21 hectares en 2025 à 45 hectares en 2026, améliorant ainsi la production alimentaire et les revenus des ménages. Au Burkina Faso, des initiatives similaires à Kaya aident les personnes déplacées à l’intérieur du pays et les communautés d’accueil à accroître la production alimentaire, à réduire les pertes après récolte et à générer des revenus.

Ces initiatives restent très modestes au regard de l’ampleur des déplacements, mais elles montrent ce qu’il est possible d’accomplir lorsque les personnes contraintes de fuir disposent des moyens nécessaires pour reconstruire leur vie dans l’attente de solutions à plus long terme.

Pour étendre ces initiatives à plus grande échelle, des investissements soutenus seront nécessaires afin de renforcer les systèmes nationaux, de développer les moyens de subsistance et de soutenir les personnes déplacées ainsi que les communautés qui les accueillent.

La crise s’étend également de manière croissante au-delà du Sahel central. En 2026, près de 500 000 réfugiés et demandeurs d’asile burkinabè avaient trouvé refuge dans les pays voisins, contre plus de 300 000 à la fin de 2025. Beaucoup ont fui vers les pays côtiers d’Afrique de l’Ouest, notamment le Bénin, la Côte d’Ivoire, le Ghana et le Togo. Plus de 334 000 Maliens sont également réfugiés à l’étranger, tandis que plus de 106 000 Nigériens sont enregistrés comme réfugiés ou demandeurs d’asile dans les pays voisins.

Pour certains, le déplacement ne prend pas fin dans les pays voisins. Lorsque la sécurité et les perspectives d’avenir restent hors de portée, des réfugiés peuvent être amenés à poursuivre leur route, souvent aux côtés de migrants, en empruntant des itinéraires dangereux vers l’Afrique du Nord et l’Europe. Cette situation souligne les conséquences régionales et internationales plus larges d’une insécurité prolongée et du manque de perspectives dans la région.

Afin de renforcer la protection et les solutions pour les réfugiés et les migrants tout au long des principaux itinéraires régionaux, le HCR travaille avec les gouvernements et ses partenaires à la mise en place de centres de services polyvalents offrant des informations essentielles, des services de conseil et d’orientation ainsi qu’une assistance de première nécessité.

Dans le même temps, les graves déficits de financement affaiblissent la réponse humanitaire alors même que les besoins continuent d’augmenter. En septembre 2026, la réponse du HCR au Sahel n'était financée qu'à hauteur de 27 % des 329,6 millions de dollars nécessaires, imposant des choix difficiles quant aux services et activités essentiels à maintenir.

Ce sous-financement compromet des activités cruciales de protection et d'assistance, notamment l'enregistrement et la délivrance de documents, l'hébergement, l'accès aux services de base et le soutien aux moyens de subsistance. Les conséquences vont bien au-delà des besoins humanitaires immédiats. Faute d’une aide suffisante et de possibilités de devenir autonomes, les réfugiés et les personnes déplacées à l’intérieur de leur pays rencontrent des difficultés croissantes pour reconstruire leur vie, tandis que les communautés d’accueil disposent de moins de ressources pour subvenir aux besoins de populations toujours plus nombreuses.

Avec près de 4 millions de personnes déplacées, l’heure est au renforcement de l’action, et non au désengagement. Les gouvernements, les partenaires du développement, les institutions financières internationales et le secteur privé doivent investir dès maintenant dans la protection, les services essentiels, les moyens de subsistance et les communautés d’accueil, tandis qu’un engagement politique soutenu reste indispensable pour répondre à l’insécurité à l’origine des déplacements.

fields.title: Nepal: A long road to recovery
fields.body:
**Kathmandu, 9 October –** “More than 32,000 children in Nepal have been affected by floods that began when a mountain of glacial ice and rock collapsed into a Himalayan river in late August. Parts of towns and villages look like war zones. Scientists warn, that as the Himalayas warm, this kind of disaster is becoming more likely. And the countries that have done least to cause it are being left to pay for it.

“Eighty-four children have been declared dead. With 5,285 people still missing, that number will, sadly, swell.

“And so, six weeks after the disaster, heartache remains daily. Sahara is 16. I met her at her technical training centre on Tuesday. Her mother was swept away by the floods and killed. Through tears, Sahara told me: "It's not nice to live without a mother."

“I asked Sahara whether she thought climate change had played a part in the disaster. She said that at school they learnt how to look after their own surroundings. Her community does what it can to protect the land around it. Sahara has done nothing to cause this crisis, yet children like her bear a disproportionate share of its consequences, from disrupted education to the loss of safety and of loves ones.

“Scientists are careful about pinning one disaster on climate change, and rightly so. But the conditions behind it are well understood. The Himalayas are warming about twice as fast as the global average. Glaciers are shrinking, permafrost is thawing, and the ice and frozen ground that hold these slopes together are weakening.

“This reaches far beyond Nepal. The Hindu Kush Himalaya holds more ice than anywhere on Earth, outside the polar regions. Two hundred and forty million people live in these mountains. Another 1.65 billion live downstream and rely on the rivers this ice feeds. That is nearly two billion people. About a quarter of humanity.

“That system is being pushed out of balance. Faster melting brings more water and more flood risk now, and serious shortages later as the glaciers disappear. Both are driven by a heating planet.

“Nepal produces only around 0.1 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions. Yet children, who are least responsible for the climate crisis, are among those bearing its heaviest consequences.

“Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) have agreed to provide finance and support to avert, minimise and address loss and damage. For countries like Nepal, these commitments must translate into practical support that reaches affected communities quickly. Such finance must be grant-based, accessible and responsive to children's needs and rights.

“What could money do *now*? Let me tell you about Shushila and her husband, Jivan.

“Jivan is deaf and does not speak. Shushila is an amputee. Together they built two businesses, a tailor's shop and a tea shop, and send their three children to fee-paying schools. I have seen photos of those shops from before the flood: bright, welcoming, full of care. And successful. They bought an apartment of their own.

“Then the flood came. Water rose more than two metres through their home and destroyed both businesses. They escaped with the clothes they were wearing, and nothing else. Shushila told me: ‘Maybe it would have been better if we weren't able to escape’.

“That is the stress and trauma brought on by inaction elsewhere in the world. And this is what climate finance is for: letting a family like this start again.

“UNICEF has supported Shushila and Jivan’s family with cash assistance. With so many needs, how did they prioritise their spending? On their children. Books, stationery and clothes.

“A one-off payment is of course not the solution. Sustained cash to this family, and many thousands like them is essential.

“Humanitarian cash is part of UNICEF’s winterization response. While we also distribute blankets, newborn kits, and warm winter clothes, cash gives people the dignity to decide for themselves what they need most this winter. Whether that is to pay the rent, to keep their girls in school, money for gas and fuel, or seed funding to restart their small shops and business. And winter is coming.

“Lastly, let’s be clear: this disaster did not begin when the water rose. Before the floods, more than half a million children in Nepal were already exposed to at least three multiple overlapping climate and environmental hazards.

“Disasters like this harm children in three ways. First, they destroy essential services. In these floods alone, 23 schools, seven health facilities and 64 water systems were damaged or destroyed. Second, they leave deep emotional scars, so psychosocial support matters as much as food, water and shelter. Third, they put a generation at risk. Children miss out on learning, and in a country where 28 per cent of young women were already married as children, girls face a greater risk of child marriage.

“Some positive news to end on. The response from Government, communities and the UN is comprehensive. I saw new bridges built just weeks after a mountain of water and rock ripped through such infrastructure. In weeks, UNICEF and partners have vaccinated more than 68,000 people against cholera, restored water to 27,000 and got thousands of children back into learning and play spaces. And we have reunited dozens (51) of children with their families.

“I saw our response in the face of smiling children in school tents, in the relief of mums with babies and newborn kits, and in children getting after-school psychological support. However, unless the world acts to reduce climate risks, we will keep returning to the same valleys after the next flood and the next landslide, and yet again find children once paying the highest price.

"That is true in Nepal, across Asia and the Pacific, and around the world.”

fields.title: UNHCR calls for urgent investment as displacement crisis deepens across Central Sahel
fields.body:
*This is a summary of what was said by Abdouraouf Gnon-Konde, UNHCR's Director of the Regional Bureau for West and Central Africa – to whom quoted text may be attributed – at the press briefing at the Palais des Nations in Geneva.*

GENEVA – UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency, is increasingly concerned about the deepening displacement crisis in the Central Sahel, with nearly 4 million people uprooted across Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger, including more than 818,000 refugees and asylum-seekers. This is roughly twice the number recorded in October 2020, when the region had more than 1.7 million internally displaced people and 365,000 refugees.

The crisis is being compounded by continued attacks affecting civilians, climate-related shocks and severe humanitarian funding shortfalls. Together, these pressures are forcing more families to flee, eroding livelihoods and limiting opportunities for displaced people to rebuild their lives, contributing to further movements within and beyond the region.

In Mali, the vast majority of refugees are from neighbouring Burkina Faso. In Koro, in the Bandiagara region, some 86,000 Burkinabè refugees had sought safety as of July 2026, following successive waves of displacement since 2025. Among them are more than 14,000 children and 6,000 women identified as being at particular risk. The refugee population is now approaching the size of the local host community, placing mounting pressure on already scarce land and water resources, overstretched health services and limited livelihood opportunities.

Climate-related shocks are adding another layer of pressure to communities already struggling with displacement and insecurity. Recurrent droughts, erratic rainfall and flooding are disrupting agricultural production, damaging homes and infrastructure, and reducing access to water and livelihoods. For families who depend heavily on farming and livestock, these shocks are further undermining their ability to support themselves.

While longer-term political solutions are pursued, much greater support is needed now for refugees, internally displaced people and the communities hosting them. More resources are urgently needed to protect those most at risk, sustain access to basic services, including education, and expand livelihood opportunities, in line with UNHCR’s [50 by 35 vision](https://www.unhcr.org/50-by-35), which aims to advance self-reliance and lasting solutions for refugees in protracted displacement by 2035.

In Koro, agricultural cooperative initiatives bringing together Burkinabè refugees and host-community members have helped expand cultivated land from 21 hectares in 2025 to 45 hectares in 2026, improving food production and household incomes. In Burkina Faso, similar support in Kaya is helping internally displaced people and host communities increase food production, reduce post-harvest losses and generate income.

These efforts remain tiny compared with the scale of displacement, but they show what can be achieved when people forced to flee are given the means to rebuild their lives while longer-term solutions are sought.

Scaling up these initiatives will require sustained investment to strengthen national systems, expand livelihood opportunities and support displaced people and the communities hosting them.

The crisis is also increasingly extending beyond the Central Sahel. In 2026, almost 500,000 Burkinabè refugees and asylum-seekers had sought safety in neighbouring countries, up from over 300,000 at the end of 2025. Many have fled to West Africa’s coastal countries, including Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana and Togo. More than 334,000 Malians are also refugees abroad, while over 106,000 Nigeriens are recorded as refugees and asylum-seekers in neighbouring countries.

For some, displacement does not end in neighbouring countries. When safety and prospects remain out of reach, refugees may move on, often alongside migrants, taking dangerous routes towards North Africa and Europe. This underscores the wider regional and international consequences of prolonged insecurity and limited opportunities closer to home.

To strengthen protection and solutions for refugees and migrants wherever they are along key routes across the region, UNHCR has been working with governments and partners to establish multi-purpose service hubs that provide critical information, counselling, referral services and essential assistance.

At the same time, severe funding shortfalls are weakening the humanitarian response just as needs continue to grow. As of September 2026, UNHCR's response in the Sahel was only 27 per cent funded, against the $329.6 million require, forcing difficult choices over which essential services and activities can be sustained.

Funding constraints are affecting critical protection and assistance, including registration and documentation, shelter, access to basic services and support for livelihoods. The consequences extend beyond immediate humanitarian needs. Without adequate assistance and opportunities to become self-reliant, refugees and internally displaced people face growing difficulties rebuilding their lives, while host communities are left with fewer resources to support increasing populations.

With nearly 4 million people displaced, this is the moment to scale up, not step back. Governments, development partners, international financial institutions and the private sector must invest now in protection, services, livelihoods and host communities, while sustained political engagement addresses the insecurity driving displacement.

**For more information, please contact:**

- In Dakar (regional), Senan Rose Fidelia Bohissou: bohissou@unhcr.org, +221 77 569 91 60

- In Geneva, Eujin Byun: byun@unhcr.org, +41 79 747 8719
